rv.q: Ms. Farrow gives a remarkable performance, so vividly felt and fully realized that you forget that she is merely reciting notes and letters.

It's one of Mr. Gurney's best plays, a tender study of thwarted love: Melissa is a scatty upper-class rebel, Andy is a stuffy upper-middle-class striver, and as they read a lifetime's worth of letters out loud, you come to know them so well that their parallel sorrows seem as familiar as your own.
With only two characters, this deceptively simple piece, for all its familiarity, is a beguiling and wrenching kaleidoscope of real emotions.
Farrow, who hasn’t been on Broadway in 34 years, is quite wonderful in the far more expressive role of the two.
After all these years, Gurney’s bittersweet love letter to an oddly matched couple who maintain an epistolary friendship for half a century can still tug at the old heartstrings.
This vintage Gurney is worth a second read.
Starve a play and you don’t have a play.
As craftily written as “Love Letters” is, it’s also static: There’s not much director Gregory Mosher can do with this setup.

What's the minimum requirement for putting on a play? Is it performers? Sets? Memorization? Surely, at a minimum, it's acting, right? More than a quarter-century after 'Love Letters' premiered, A.R. Gurney's charming ditty of a play has landed on Broadway with virtually none of the characteristics of what you might expect in a play.
The Pulitzer-nominated “Love Letters,” by comparison, is a near-classic.
Bergen and Dennehy make beautiful music together in this simple but affecting two-hander about a lifetime correspondence between friends who become lovers.
I can only answer based on the first company-Brian Dennehy and Mia Farrow-and the response is an unqualified yes.
Gurney's play, as revived at the Brooks Atkinson under the direction of Gregory Mosher, is smart, delightful, and moving.
Director Gregory Mosher's superlative new Broadway revival has attracted an impressive roster of performers who will rotate through the production in monthly increments.
He finds heartbreak in the simplest of declarations.
Mia Farrow is delicious as Melissa at all ages. Her young child is a frisky thing so earnest she snatches at your heart before you have a chance to cover it.
Mia Farrow in particular feels ideally cast; it’s hard to imagine somebody who would do a better job as Melissa Gardner (although I am willing to reappraise if and when I see the other performers.)
Their missed opportunities for connection seem as contrived as the moments when, against all odds, they finally do connect.
Gurney may have written a caricature, but Farrow colors it with a heartfelt performance.

cn.t: Gurney's minimal two-hander divides critics: some find the script charming and emotionally rich, elevated by strong star performances, while others deem the bare-bones staging deflating and the premise slight for Broadway.

vs.sum: The Lena Horne Theatre offers good sightlines from most seats, with clear views even from the rear mezzanine. The sound quality is well-balanced across the theater. However, the seating is quite tight, especially for taller patrons, which affects comfort. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its historic architecture and restored interior, providing a charming atmosphere.

acc.note: Step-free entry and Orchestra. 5 wheelchair seats. No elevators.
